title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 106
paragraphs: When the Greeks had slain most of the barbarians — some in battle, others in their flight — they set fire to the ships and the whole wall, having first brought out the spoils onto the shore; and among the rest they found some stores of money. Having set fire to the wall and the ships, they sailed away; and when they came to Samos, the Greeks deliberated about removing the inhabitants of Ionia, and considered where they ought to settle them in those parts of Greece under their control, leaving Ionia to the barbarians. For it was clear to them that, on the one hand, it was impossible for them always to be stationed as guards to protect the Ionians; and on the other, if they were not so stationed, they had no hope that the Ionians would escape unpunished from the Persians. The Peloponnesians in authority thought it good to remove the inhabitants of the trading ports belonging to those peoples of Greece who had sided with the Medes, and to give that land to the Ionians to dwell in. But the Athenians did not think it good for the inhabitants of Ionia to be removed at all, nor that the Peloponnesians should deliberate about Athenian colonies. As these resisted the proposal vehemently, the Peloponnesians gave way. So the outcome was that they joined as allies to their league the Samians, Chians, Lesbians, and the other islanders who happened to be serving with the Greeks, binding them by pledges and oaths to remain faithful and not withdraw from the league. Having bound them by oaths, they sailed to break up the bridges, for they supposed they would find them still stretched across the straits.
These, then, were sailing toward the Hellespont.
